output.title: Designing against eval drift starts with a threshold
output.body:
If you are automating a recurring workflow, eval drift is not a theory problem. It is the point where a system that looked fine on your sample stops matching the work it sees in real life. For a small business, that often shows up in inbox handling, invoices, or lead follow-up.

The practical move is to define the workflow, the measurable outcome, and the stop rule before you automate. For example, if you are classifying customer emails or invoices, decide what “correct enough” means and what level of manual review means the system needs a reset. The percentages below are only an illustration: if a workflow starts sending 5% of items to manual review and later that rises to 15%, that is a signal to pause and inspect what changed. Not a magic number. Just a guardrail.

Human approval still matters for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Eval drift design should not mean a machine quietly keeps going while the owner assumes everything is still on track. It means the system is built to alert you when confidence drops or patterns change, so you stay in charge.

One practical next step: write down two questions for any workflow you want to automate — “How will I know if this stops working?” and “What decision do I need to keep?” If you cannot answer those clearly, the automation is not ready for a real workflow.
